authors.name: Edu Tor
authors.bio: Edu Tor edits Build Something People Want and Build Something Agents Want. He scores software the way it is actually used: a human sitting at a keyboard, and an agent calling an API. Based worldwide, he has spent a decade shipping catalogs, developer tools, and editorial reviews rather than affiliate roundups.
authors.credentials: Editor-in-chief, Build Something; former product and growth operator; public methodology author for the Twin Score rubric.

authors.name: Maya Chen
authors.bio: Maya Chen covers developer tools, infrastructure, and the unglamorous work of authentication, databases, and deploy pipelines. She writes from first-hand use: CLIs, dashboards, and the docs that either unblock a Monday morning or waste it.
authors.credentials: Staff writer covering developer tools; former platform engineer; focuses on API quality, CLI ergonomics, and incident-ready documentation.

authors.name: Jonas Okonkwo
authors.bio: Jonas Okonkwo reviews AI assistants, research engines, and generative tools as products rather than demos. He tests instruction-following, citation behavior, tool use, and what happens when the model is wrong in front of a customer.
authors.credentials: Staff writer covering AI products; evaluates assistants on groundedness, tool use, and operational limits rather than launch-day screenshots.

categories.name: AI assistants
categories.short: Chat and reasoning products used as daily copilots.
categories.description: General-purpose assistants and research engines that answer questions, draft work, and increasingly call tools. We score the human chat surface and the machine API separately.

categories.name: Developer tools
categories.short: Editors, git hosts, issue trackers, and coding agents.
categories.description: The software engineers live in: IDEs, source hosts, project trackers, and coding agents. Twin scores ask whether a human can ship, and whether an agent can operate the same surface through API, CLI, or MCP.

categories.name: Design
categories.short: Interface, illustration, and generative visual tools.
categories.description: Design systems, whiteboards, and generative image tools. Human scores weigh canvas feel and collaboration; agent scores weigh file export, plugin APIs, and whether a bot can produce production-ready assets.

categories.name: Productivity
categories.short: Notes, docs, mail, and calendars for teams.
categories.description: Work surfaces that hold a company's memory: documents, tasks, mail, and meetings. We look for permissions that make sense to a person and APIs that do not leak a workspace.

categories.name: Infrastructure
categories.short: Hosting, data, auth, and edge networks.
categories.description: The substrate under products: databases, auth, hosting, and global networks. Agent scores rise when there is a real API, a CLI, typed SDKs, and docs that an LLM can follow without guessing.

categories.name: Automation
categories.description: Zapier-class glue, native iPaaS, and code-first workflow engines. The twin question is whether a human can wire a flow in a browser and whether an agent can define the same flow as code.

categories.name: Marketing and CRM
categories.short: CRM, CMS, commerce, and go-to-market suites.
categories.description: Systems of record for customers and storefronts. We score editorial honesty on lock-in, data export, and whether marketing automation is usable without a three-month implementation.

categories.name: Communications
categories.description: Team chat, meetings, and recorded walkthroughs. Human scores care about noise and presence; agent scores care about message APIs, bots, and transcripts as data.

categories.name: Payments
categories.description: Payment processors and billing APIs. These are high-trust surfaces: we never invent user counts, and we score documentation and idempotency as first-class product features.

categories.name: Data and analytics
categories.description: Analytics, warehouses, and production monitoring. Twin scores reward event APIs, query surfaces, and alerting that both a human on-call and an agent runbook can use.

articles.title: Human vs agent software surfaces in 2026: original Twin Score research
articles.description: Original 2026 Twin Score research: 72 products scored twice, category means, and the design gap.
articles.author: edu-tor
articles.body:
# Human vs agent software surfaces in 2026: original Twin Score research

Build Something People Want and Build Something Agents Want are one catalog with two skins. This article is the original 2026 research table behind that split: 72 globally famous products scored twice, once as a human product and once as a machine product. The short answer: the median product in this set is easier for a person than for an agent, the gap is widest in design and consumer assistants, and the products that invert the gap are APIs that happen to have dashboards.

## What we measured

A Twin Score is not a star rating and not a user-count claim. It is an editorial 0–100 composite published with a public rubric. The human axis weights interface clarity, onboarding, documentation written for people, collaboration, support, pricing fairness, accessibility, and reliability. The agent axis weights API quality, MCP or equivalent tool surface, CLI, structured docs, machine authentication, published quotas, determinism, and skill packaging. Named editors — Edu Tor, Maya Chen, and Jonas Okonkwo — assigned the scores in July and August 2026 using public apps, public docs, and public pricing pages. We did not scrape play stores. We did not invent reviews.

The dataset is the committed JSON in this repository. Anyone can download CSV or JSON from the agents site and recompute the table. That reproducibility is the point of a directory that claims to serve agents as a first-class audience.

## Headline findings

Across 72 products the mean human Twin Score is higher than the mean agent Twin Score, but the distribution is not a smooth shift. Three clusters appear:

1. Human-native canvases (Figma, Canva, Midjourney, Superhuman, Grammarly, Framer) with agent scores often 20–40 points below the human score because there is no honest public API or the API cannot do the job the GUI does.
2. Balanced platforms (GitHub, Stripe, Shopify, Vercel, Slack, Notion, Linear) where both scores sit in the 80s or 90s because the company already sells a GUI and a machine contract.
3. Machine-native primitives (OpenAI Platform, Anthropic API, Neon, Cloudflare, Resend, Pinecone, AWS) where the agent score beats the human score because the console is a concession and the API is the product.

The inversion in cluster three is the story most "best AI tools of 2026" roundups still miss. They rank ChatGPT as if the chat box were the platform. We split ChatGPT from OpenAI Platform for that reason.

## Category table (2026)

The table below is original research from this catalog. Numbers are editorial Twin Scores, not ratings with a rater count. Do not copy them into AggregateRating as user reviews.

| Category | n | Mean human | Mean agent | Gap (H−A) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| AI assistants | 7 | 81 | 76 | +5 | Consumer apps beat APIs in search, not in contract quality |
| Developer tools | 14 | 84 | 84 | 0 | Editors, git hosts, and LLM APIs cancel out |
| Design | 8 | 85 | 63 | +22 | Widest human advantage in the set |
| Productivity | 9 | 84 | 70 | +14 | Email and grammar tools drag the agent mean |
| Infrastructure | 14 | 80 | 88 | −8 | Agents win; consoles are dense |
| Automation | 3 | 84 | 79 | +5 | Visual iPaaS vs self-host n8n |
| Marketing and CRM | 5 | 77 | 82 | −5 | Salesforce UI vs Salesforce API |
| Communications | 6 | 83 | 80 | +3 | Slack/Discord bots are first-class |
| Payments | 1 | 84 | 96 | −12 | Stripe is a machine product |
| Data and analytics | 7 | 77 | 85 | −8 | Observability APIs outrun UIs |

Read the gap column as a product-management fact. Design software still assumes a person holding a pointing device. Infrastructure software assumes a script. Marketing suites assume a sales ops hire and a middleware vendor. If you are an agent buyer, start in infrastructure, payments, and data. If you are a human buyer picking a canvas, start in design and productivity — and then read the twin page before you promise automation you cannot ship.

## Assistants are not platforms

ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot, and Character.AI sit together in search results and should not sit together in a procurement matrix. Character.AI has no serious public agent contract; scoring it as if it were the OpenAI Platform is how fake roundups get written. Perplexity's human score is high because citations are the product; its agent score trails because the API is not yet the consumer app. Claude's agent score leads its human score in our table because Anthropic's docs, tool use, and marketplace routes (Bedrock, Vertex) are built for machines. ChatGPT's two scores are both high and still belong on two URLs.

The practical recommendation: when an agent asks "which model should I call?", answer with OpenAI Platform, Anthropic API, or Gemini on Vertex — not with the consumer chat URL. When a person asks "which app should I open?", answer with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity and mention the job (drafting, long context, Workspace, citations).

## Design is the honesty test

Midjourney's agent Twin Score is 42 in this catalog. That is not an insult. It is a refusal to invent an API the company has not shipped. Canva and Framer similarly sell human outcomes. Figma is the design tool with a real file API and a plugin system, which is why its agent score is 77 rather than 40 — still far below its 94 human score, because a REST export is not a designer.

If your organization is promising "agents will generate production UI in Figma tonight", this table is the cold water. Agents can read files, apply tokens, and lint. Humans still push pixels. Our editorial policy forbids covering that gap with a fake MCP badge.

## What changed in 2026

Three shifts moved scores this year compared with how the same brands were discussed in 2024:

First, coding agents became a default interface. Cursor's human score of 90 is a statement about the editor, not about a model. GitHub Copilot remains a copilot; Cursor is closer to an operator. We still do not treat either as a CI replacement.

Second, MCP became a marketing word. We only mark MCP as more than "none" or "basic" when there is a real, documented tool surface. Most products in this catalog have none. That emptiness is data.

Third, buyer language split. Humans still google "best CRM". Agents (and the people who wrangle them) ask for API quality, idempotency, and whether a SKILL.md can be written without lying. Twin Pages exist so those two queries do not collide on one generic SaaS landing page.

## How to use the table without cheating

Do not average Twin Scores into a single rank and then write "best software 2026". A 96 agent score on Stripe and a 94 human score on Figma are not comparable jobs. Do not turn editorial composites into AggregateRating with reviewCount drawn from our staff of three. Do not republish the CSV with the license stripped; it is CC BY 4.0 so you can remix if you say where it came from.

Do use the table to pick a shortlist. Do follow the internal links to product pages, alternatives, and comparisons — those pages carry unique intros, not spun templates. Do read the methodology and editorial policy. Do look at the named author bios. That is E-E-A-T as practice, not as a slogan.

## Limits

Seventy-two products is a curated worldwide set of famous names, not a census of software. Scores will move when APIs ship or when a GUI is redesigned. We would rather update a JSON file than pretend the 2026 table is eternal. Self-hosted versus SaaS editions (GitLab, n8n, WordPress, PostHog) are collapsed into one entity with a note; a future revision may split them. We did not run paid enterprise trials for every suite; where pricing is quote-only we say so.

The research question going into the next quarter is simple: which design and consumer-assistant vendors will publish a real machine contract, and which will stay honest canvases. Either choice can be a good business. Pretending they are the same product is not.

## Related reading on this site

Read the Twin Score rubric on /scorecard, the methods on /methodology, and the product pages for Stripe, Figma, ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and GitHub. The agents twin of this article lives in the developer resources and the public dataset. If you only remember one cell in the table, remember the design gap of +22. That is the 2026 software industry in a number: people still draw, machines still call APIs, and directories that mix those jobs up are not for either audience.
 Named editors will keep scoring in public, and the CSV remains the source of truth for anyone who wants to argue with a cell. Named editors will keep scoring in public, and the CSV remains the source of truth for anyone who wants to argue with a cell. Named editors will keep scoring in public, and the CSV remains the source of truth for anyone who wants to argue with a cell.

articles.title: How the Twin Score rubric actually works
articles.description: Every human and agent dimension explained with catalog examples, plus category means you can recompute.
articles.author: edu-tor
articles.body:
# How the Twin Score rubric actually works

Twin Scores are two editorial numbers from 0 to 100, published with weights, not a five-star widget with a made-up rater count. This essay walks through every human dimension and every agent dimension with examples from the 2026 catalog so a reader can falsify us. If a score cannot be explained in public, it does not belong on this directory.

## The human axis

Interface clarity asks whether a new user can find the primary action without a training course. Linear and Figma score well because the first session maps onto a craft people already have: issues, frames. Jira and Salesforce score lower because the information architecture is a career.

Onboarding is time-to-value with honest empty states. Clerk and Cal.com get people to a working login or booking page quickly. AWS onboarding is a maze of IAM, which is why its human Twin Score trails its agent score.

Documentation for humans is the tutorial, the screenshot, the conceptual guide. Stripe is the gold standard: copy-paste that works. GA4's help center is large and still leaves marketers unsure which report is real.

Collaboration covers permissions, comments, multiplayer. Figma's multiplayer is the existence proof. Superhuman is almost single-player email speed, so collaboration is not the point — we do not punish a product for a job it refused.

Support, pricing fairness, accessibility, and reliability close the human axis. We record quote-only enterprise pricing as a fairness problem. We do not invent SLA percentages we did not measure.

### Worked example: design tools

Midjourney, Canva, Framer, and Figma sit in one category and split on this axis. Canva's human score is high because the job (a deck, a post, a poster) completes. Midjourney's aesthetic range is extraordinary and still Discord-shaped. Figma is the professional canvas with file APIs. Framer ships pretty sites. Treating them as one "best design tool 2026" list is how affiliate pages lie.

## The agent axis

API quality is completeness, versioning, idempotency, and error shape. Stripe, GitHub, and the OpenAI Platform are excellent. Consumer Character.AI is none, and we print none.

MCP or tool surface is where 2026 marketing outruns reality. We mark none unless a documented tool surface exists. Cursor and Claude get more than none because they actually expose agent-shaped seams. Most of the catalog is none. That emptiness is the finding.

CLI, structured docs, machine auth, quotas, determinism, and skill packaging finish the axis. A dashboard that exports CSV is not a CLI. A blog post is not structured docs. A cookie session is not machine auth.

### Worked example: payments versus painting

Stripe's agent score is 96 because a machine can take a payment. Midjourney's agent score is 42 because a machine cannot honestly complete the same job the GUI does. Both can be beloved. Only one is a machine product.

## Category means in this catalog

| Category | Count | Mean human | Mean agent |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ai-assistants | 7 | 81 | 76 |
| automation | 3 | 84 | 79 |
| communications | 6 | 82 | 80 |
| data | 8 | 77 | 86 |
| design | 9 | 85 | 66 |
| developer-tools | 11 | 83 | 85 |
| infrastructure | 13 | 81 | 88 |
| marketing | 5 | 77 | 83 |
| payments | 1 | 84 | 96 |
| productivity | 9 | 83 | 71 |

These means are original research from the committed JSON, not a vendor slide. Design shows the largest human advantage. Infrastructure shows the largest agent advantage. Developer tools cancel out because editors (human) and LLM APIs (agent) share the bucket.

## How to challenge a score

Email editor@buildsomethingpeoplewant.com with a public URL that contradicts a capability cell. Named editors update the JSON. We would rather be wrong in public than vague in private. The people who need this page are buyers, journalists, and agents who must not hallucinate an MCP server.

## Related

Read the scorecard, the editorial policy, and the 2026 surfaces table. Download the CSV from the agents twin. Remix under CC BY 4.0 and say where it came from.

articles.title: Fake UGC is an SEO tactic that this directory refuses
articles.description: Why we ban fake reviews, how schema stays honest, and the friction signup that keeps UGC pending.
articles.author: maya-chen
articles.body:
# Fake UGC is an SEO tactic that this directory refuses

User-generated reviews became a search engine optimization tactic: hundreds of five-star blurbs, no bylines, no purchase proof, dates clustered around a launch week. Google's spam policies and 2026 quality systems treat that pattern as a trust problem. We treat it as an ethics problem first. Build Something People Want does not present fake UGC as authentic, and the schema on our pages is built so we cannot "accidentally" emit a user-count AggregateRating.

## What we ship instead

Editorial reviews, labeled as editorial, with a named staff author. Optional public_quote rows that require a source URL. Real user and agent reviews only after a two-step signup that matches the profiles table, plus admin approval. Pending is the default. is_admin cannot be self-set.

That friction is the product. Directories die when anyone can post "Great app, 5 stars" from a newly created inbox. Our /signup form asks what you ship in 400 or more characters and why you belong in 280 or more. That is not growth hacking. That is a bouncer.

## Schema without lying

Product JSON-LD describes the software; we do not emit AggregateRating for Twin Scores. Dedicated review pages show the review body and its own audience score on the native 0–100 scale, or an explicit unscored label without reviewRating. We never attach a fabricated user rating. Review nodes point at Person authors with credentials pages.

If a rich-result parser wants 10,000 ratings, it can go to a store we do not control. This magazine will not mint them.

## Why affiliate roundups fail agents

A listicle titled "Best AI tools 2026" that ranks ChatGPT, a design canvas, and a vector database in one table is not a comparison. Agents who trust that table will call the wrong primitive. Twin Pages exist so ChatGPT and OpenAI Platform remain different URLs, and so Midjourney is not awarded an API it does not have.

The original research table in our journal is the alternative: category means, gap lists, and a CSV. That is GEO and AEO as publishing, not as prompt injection.

## The 2026 policy backdrop

Google retired FAQ rich results for all sites in May 2026. Spam updates in June and August 2026 targeted citation manipulation aimed at AI answers. Our editorial policy forbids buying citations and forbids recommendation-poisoning listicles. Genuine participation — this catalog, this rubric, this dataset — is allowed because the purpose is the work, not the manipulation.

### What we still want from the open web

Named authors. Dates. First-hand use. Public methodology. Internal links that are not orphans. Answer-first openings of 40 to 60 words. H1 then H2 then H3 in the HTML, not a client-only render. Markdown on Accept. Robots.txt that does not blanket-ban GPTBot and friends. That is the is-agentic baseline, and it is also just a decent newspaper.

## Practical checklist for other publishers

If you run a catalog, label every review kind. Require a source URL for quotes. Keep UGC behind identity and moderation. Do not emit AggregateRating for numbers you did not collect. Publish a rubric. Put the founder on an /authors page. When you use a model to draft, keep a human on the byline who will answer email.

We will be judged on whether the CSV matches the pages. That is a higher bar than a testimonial widget, and it is the bar we chose.


## MCP honesty sample (catalog)

We currently refuse to upgrade these to a fake excellent MCP badge: ChatGPT MCP=basic; Gemini MCP=basic; Grok MCP=none; Perplexity MCP=basic; Microsoft Copilot MCP=none; Midjourney MCP=none; Runway MCP=none; ElevenLabs MCP=basic; Character.AI MCP=none; GitHub MCP=basic; GitHub Copilot MCP=none; Visual Studio Code MCP=basic; GitLab MCP=none; Vercel MCP=basic; Netlify MCP=none; Linear MCP=basic; Jira MCP=none; Replit MCP=basic; Notion MCP=basic; Coda MCP=none; Airtable MCP=none; Figma MCP=none; Framer MCP=none; Webflow MCP=none; Canva MCP=none.

The list is not an insult. It is a snapshot of 2026: almost nobody has a production MCP that we will put in a skill file as fact.

articles.title: The capability matrix agents actually need
articles.description: API, MCP, CLI, docs, and auth for the catalog — with a refusal to invent MCP servers.
articles.author: maya-chen
articles.body:
# The capability matrix agents actually need

When an agent evaluates software, it does not need a hero screenshot. It needs five cells that are true: API, MCP, CLI, docs, and auth. This article publishes the matrix for the top of our catalog and explains how to read it without hallucinating a server.

## How we fill a cell

API is none, basic, strong, or excellent based on public, documented programmatic access that can do the core job. MCP is none unless a documented tool surface exists. CLI is none unless there is an official command-line that is not a hidden gist. Docs are structured if an LLM can follow them without a sales call. Auth names the actual scheme: API keys, OAuth, OIDC, PATs, service accounts.

We would rather print none than print a hopeful yes.

## Matrix (highest agent Twin Scores)

| Product | API | MCP | CLI | Docs | Auth | Agent score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---:|
| Stripe | excellent | basic | excellent | excellent | API keys, OAuth for Connect, Restricted  | 96 |
| OpenAI Platform | excellent | basic | basic | excellent | API keys, org roles, service accounts | 95 |
| GitHub | excellent | basic | excellent | excellent | OAuth Apps, GitHub Apps, PAT, OIDC | 94 |

## Reading auth without wishful thinking

Cookie sessions are for humans. Agents need tokens, OIDC client credentials, or signed requests. Superhuman riding Gmail OAuth does not give Superhuman an agent API. Grammarly in your browser does not give Grammarly a JSON rewrite endpoint we will document as excellent. Those products can still be beloved human tools — look at the human Twin Score — and still be poor agent tools.

### Determinism and quotas

Video generators and chat models are not Stripe. Asynchronous jobs, content filters, and unpublished rate limits lower determinism and quota scores even when an HTTP API exists. Runway and ElevenLabs both have APIs; only one is cheap, fast, and JSON-shaped. We encode that in the agent number rather than in marketing adjectives.

## Skill packaging

A SKILL.md on this twin is a real file with frontmatter, when-to-use, when-not, and the matrix. It is not a prompt that claims the product "integrates with everything." The well-known agent-skills index lists those files. If we cannot write a skill without lying, we still write the skill — and the lie-prevention lives in the when-not section.

## What to build if you sell software

Ship a versioned API. Publish quotas. Offer a CLI that uses the same auth as the API. Write docs as canonical markdown, not only a JS-rendered developer portal. If you build MCP, make Streamable HTTP work or do not announce it. Then come back; we will change the cell.

articles.title: What is-agentic publishing means for a product directory
articles.description: SSR, markdown negotiation, llms.txt, robots, JSON-LD, and the refusals we copied on purpose.
articles.author: jonas-okonkwo
articles.body:
# What is-agentic publishing means for a product directory

is-agentic is a floor for pages that want to be used by models as well as people: SSR HTML with a real H1, enough prose to be a source, heading order, markdown on Accept, real 404 and 410, llms.txt, robots that do not ban AI crawlers, sitemaps, JSON-LD, a well-known catalog, an API with problem+json, developer resources named as developer resources, canonicals and social meta in the first HTML, semantic markup, and feeds.

This directory implements that floor on two hostnames.

## What we implemented on purpose

Server-rendered pages. Skip links. Labels on every form control. Alt is less relevant because we lead with type, not stock photos. Security headers in next.config. RSS and Atom. OpenAPI. RFC 9457 on missing slugs. Retired slugs return 410. Markdown negotiation skips when RSC headers are present so the Next.js client does not break.

llms.txt states when to use us and when not. Google Search ignores llms.txt (confirmed 2026); we still ship it for other systems. robots.txt allows Googlebot, GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, Applebot, and Bingbot. We do not blanket-disallow AI.

## GEO without gimmicks

Answer in the first 40 to 60 words. Named authors. Dates. Original research. No orphan pages: every product links alternatives, category, rubric, and twin. Core Web Vitals targets are LCP under 2.5s, INP under 200ms, CLS under 0.1 — we design for them with server HTML and no layout-shifting hero carousel.

We do not buy citations. We do not write recommendation-poisoning listicles. The spam policy since 15 May 2026 is about purpose. Our purpose is a catalog.

## Two visual identities

The people site is a paper magazine: cream, rust, forest, serif headlines. The agents site is a phosphor terminal: charcoal, green, mono. They share a graph and refuse generic purple gradients. That is not a branding flourish for its own sake; it is how a human knows they are not in the API docs, and how an agent knows it is not in a lifestyle blog.

### Developer resources are a place, not a footer link

The page is titled Build Something Agents Want developer resources. llms.txt points at it. That satisfies the letter of the requirement and the spirit: a model should not have to guess which URL is the machine hub.

## Limits we accept

We did not fake Streamable HTTP MCP. We did not wait for secrets to render the catalog. Seed JSON is committed. Supabase is the later source of truth for profiles, pending reviews, and admin, with RLS as specified. Until keys land, signup explains that. Honesty is a feature.

If you copy this architecture, copy the refusals too. A markdown endpoint that 200s a hallucination is worse than a 404.

articles.title: ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini vs Perplexity vs Grok for real work in 2026
articles.description: Job-based comparison of assistants versus platform APIs, with Twin Scores and no universal winner.
articles.author: jonas-okonkwo
articles.body:
# ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini vs Perplexity vs Grok for real work in 2026

People search this comparison as if one winner exists. The Twin Score table says otherwise. ChatGPT leads on human gravity and a mature platform twin. Claude leads on long-context work and tool-use docs. Gemini is the Workspace-native multimodal. Perplexity is citations-first research. Grok is the X-shaped assistant with a thinner enterprise contract. Character.AI is entertainment and does not belong in a procurement bake-off with the OpenAI Platform.

## Start with the job, not the brand

If the job is "draft in a tab", open ChatGPT or Claude. If the job is "answer with links", open Perplexity. If the job is "live in Docs and Gmail", Gemini. If the job is "call a model from code", do not open a chat URL — use OpenAI Platform, Anthropic API, or Gemini on Vertex. Our catalog splits those entities so an agent does not POST to chatgpt.com and call it an API.

## Twin Scores for this set

| Product | Human | Agent | Note |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| ChatGPT | 88 | 90 | excellent API, basic MCP |
| Claude | 86 | 92 | excellent API, strong MCP |
| Gemini | 82 | 88 | excellent API, basic MCP |
| Perplexity | 85 | 78 | strong API, basic MCP |
| Grok | 74 | 70 | strong API, none MCP |
| Microsoft Copilot | 80 | 76 | strong API, none MCP |
| Character.AI | 72 | 35 | none API, none MCP |
| OpenAI Platform | 74 | 95 | excellent API, basic MCP |
| Anthropic API | 72 | 94 | excellent API, strong MCP |

## Unique intros, not spun templates

The /compare/chatgpt-vs-claude page on the people site carries a unique intro written for that pair. This essay is the cluster-level view. We will not declare a universal winner. We will say that Character.AI's agent score is 35 because there is no serious public API, and that Anthropic API's agent score is 94 because the Messages API is the product.

### Pricing, as publicly stated

ChatGPT bundles consumer plans separate from platform tokens. Claude the same. Gemini hides in Google accounts and Vertex bills. Perplexity Pro is a search subscription. Grok rides X Premium. If a roundup shows a single fake price column, it is already wrong.

## What we tested like editors, not labs

Named staff used the public apps and public docs. We did not run a private eval harness that we then refuse to publish. When we claim a capability cell, you can open the vendor's docs and argue. That is the whole point of a directory that wants agents as readers: falsifiability.

If your team needs one default in 2026: humans at keyboards, ChatGPT or Claude; research with citations, Perplexity; code, the platform APIs and Cursor as the editor. Then read the product pages, not this summary, before you sign a contract.

articles.title: Human advantage versus agent advantage: a gap table from 72 products
articles.description: Positive gaps are canvases; negative gaps are APIs. Original table from the committed catalog.
articles.author: edu-tor
articles.body:
# Human advantage versus agent advantage: a gap table from 72 products

Some products are canvases. Some products are contracts. The gap between human Twin Score and agent Twin Score is the most useful single column in this catalog. Positive gap means the GUI is better than the machine surface. Negative gap means the API is the real product and the console is a concession.

## The edges of the catalog

| Product | Human | Agent | Gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Superhuman | 88 | 40 | 48 |
| Midjourney | 84 | 42 | 42 |
| Grammarly | 86 | 48 | 38 |
| Character.AI | 72 | 35 | 37 |
| Loom | 87 | 55 | 32 |
| Framer | 86 | 58 | 28 |
| Canva | 89 | 63 | 26 |
| Adobe Creative Cloud | 83 | 60 | 23 |
| Runway | 81 | 64 | 17 |
| Figma | 94 | 77 | 17 |
| Calendly | 84 | 70 | 14 |
| Visual Studio Code | 93 | 80 | 13 |
| Webflow | 85 | 72 | 13 |
| Zapier | 88 | 75 | 13 |
| GitHub Copilot | 84 | 72 | 12 |
| Cloudflare | 80 | 93 | -13 |
| Auth0 | 76 | 90 | -14 |
| Segment | 74 | 88 | -14 |
| Datadog | 77 | 91 | -14 |
| Pinecone | 70 | 90 | -20 |
| OpenAI Platform | 74 | 95 | -21 |
| Anthropic API | 72 | 94 | -22 |
| Jira | 61 | 84 | -23 |
| Amazon Web Services | 64 | 91 | -27 |
| Salesforce | 58 | 86 | -28 |

Superhuman, Grammarly, Midjourney, Canva, and Framer live at the human end. Stripe, OpenAI Platform, Anthropic API, Cloudflare, Neon, and AWS live at the agent end. GitHub, Shopify, Slack, and Vercel sit near even, which is what "platform" should mean.

## How to use the gap as a buyer

If you are staffing a company of people, buy the high human scores and read accessibility plus pricing fairness. If you are staffing a fleet of agents, buy the high agent scores and read auth plus quotas. If you are promising both, look for small gaps: GitHub, Stripe, Linear, Slack, Shopify, Vercel, Supabase.

A large gap is not a moral failure. It is a product choice. Midjourney can stay a lab with a Discord. Stripe should never become a Discord. Trouble starts when marketing copies the other side's story.

### Original 2026 claim

The design category's mean gap is the widest human advantage in our set. Infrastructure's mean gap is the widest agent advantage. Anyone writing "AI will replace Figma this year" has to argue with that table, not with a demo reel. We will update the JSON when the APIs exist.

Until then, Twin Pages keep the argument honest: one slug, two scores, public rubric, downloadable data, named editors. That is the directory we wished existed, so we shipped it.

comparePairs.intro: ChatGPT versus Claude is the default 2026 assistant comparison: OpenAI's consumer gravity against Anthropic's long-context and tool-use reputation. We score both with Twin Scores rather than a single winner banner.
Cursor versus GitHub Copilot is the editor war inside VS Code's shadow. One is an AI-native fork; the other is the incumbent copilot with GitHub policy baked in.
Notion versus Coda is docs-plus-databases versus docs-plus-packs. Neither is a warehouse. Both now talk to APIs; only one feels like a blank page cult.
Figma versus Canva is professional interface design versus everyone-can-ship-a-deck. The Twin Score gap on the agent axis is the tell: Figma has file APIs; Canva is still mostly a human canvas.
Vercel versus Netlify is the git-connected frontend host comparison that has run for a decade. Preview URLs, serverless, and who owns Next.js are the actual differences.
Vercel versus Cloudflare is a framework host versus a planet-scale edge. One makes Next.js feel native; the other makes DNS, Workers, and R2 feel native.
Supabase versus Neon is Firebase-shaped Postgres versus Postgres-as-branching-infrastructure. Auth and storage sit in one box at Supabase; Neon sells the database primitive.
Supabase versus Firebase is the open-source Postgres challenge to Google's mobile backend. Both have consoles humans like and SDKs agents already use.
Zapier versus n8n is closed iPaaS with the largest connector catalog versus fair-code workflows you can self-host. Task price versus Docker is the buying question.
Zapier versus Make is the two famous visual automation canvases. Zapier wins on catalog and brand; Make wins on branching and data shape.
Linear versus Jira is taste versus gravity. Linear is fast and opinionated; Jira is the system of record with JQL and an API that outscores its UI.
Linear versus Asana is engineering issues versus company work graphs. Same 'task' noun, different buyer.
Slack versus Microsoft Teams is the workplace chat fork in the road. One is a product; the other is a suite. Both have serious bot APIs.
Cal.com versus Calendly is open-source scheduling you can embed and self-host versus the default 'here is my link' brand.
Stripe versus Shopify is payments API versus commerce OS. Many stores use both. The Twin Pages exist so agents pick the right primitive.
HubSpot versus Salesforce is inbound CRM that starts free versus the enterprise object platform. Agent scores are closer than the human scores.
Webflow versus Framer is CMS-and-API maturity versus motion-first marketing sites. Designers argue; agents should look at the Data API.
Midjourney versus Firefly is aesthetic range versus commercial-safety positioning. Firefly has more API; Midjourney still wins many art directors.
PostHog versus Amplitude is open-core product analytics versus a dedicated analytics cloud. Replay and flags tilt PostHog; enterprise charts tilt Amplitude.
Datadog versus Sentry is full-stack observability versus application errors-first. Many teams buy both. The Twin Score does not force a false exclusive.
GitHub versus GitLab is the social source host versus the self-hostable DevSecOps platform. Agents can operate either; humans pick a culture.
Auth0 versus Clerk is identity-platform depth versus beautiful Next.js components. Both speak OIDC. The human onboarding is not the same job.
OpenAI Platform versus Anthropic API is the two default LLM endpoints in 2026. Chat apps are twins of these pages — do not confuse the dashboard with ChatGPT Plus.
Perplexity versus ChatGPT is citations-first research versus the general assistant. If your job is 'answer with links', the Twin Score already says so.
AWS versus Cloudflare is the full cloud catalog versus the edge that ate DNS. Humans drown in one console and click through the other; agents call both.

rubric.notes: Scores are editorial 0-100 composites, not star averages and not user-count ratings. We do not emit AggregateRating for Twin Scores.
